title: First seizure
summary: Explore a first seizure, witness history and immediate priorities.

aim.text: Assess history taking after a first seizure, using a witness account to separate seizure from syncope and other mimics, and giving safe advice.

candidateInstructions.text: You are the emergency doctor. Mr Tom Walker, 24, was brought in by ambulance after a collapse at work. He is now alert, observations are normal and glucose is 5.9. His colleague Anna saw the event and is with him. Take a focused history from both. Do not examine. At the end, summarise and state your initial plan.

items: Tom: felt odd (rising feeling in the stomach, strange smell), then woke on the floor with a sore tongue and wet trousers. Headache and aching since.
Anna: he went stiff, then jerked all over for about two minutes, eyes open, lips blue, did not respond. Bit the side of his tongue. Confused for about 20 minutes. Did not hit his head hard.
No fever or neck stiffness. Three hours of sleep and heavy drinking the night before.
No previous seizures, jerks or blank spells. No drugs, medicines or allergies. No family history.
Office worker, lives with flatmates, drives to work, plays football.
Concern if asked: "Do I have epilepsy? Can I still drive? Will it happen again?"

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: Hello, I am Dr Shah, one of the emergency doctors. Can you confirm your name and date of birth?

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.text: Tom Walker, 9th March 2002.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: Could you tell me what happened today, in your own words?

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.text: I remember feeling odd, then waking on the floor. My tongue is sore and I am wet.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: Thank you. Is there anything else?

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.text: My head aches and I am achy all over.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: Anna, you saw it. Can you describe what happened from the start?

lines.speaker: Colleague
lines.text: He went stiff, then jerked all over for about two minutes. His lips went blue and he did not respond. He bit his tongue.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: How long was he confused afterwards? Did he injure himself when he fell?

lines.speaker: Colleague
lines.text: About twenty minutes. He did not hit his head hard.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: Tom, what did you feel just before? Any sweating, dizziness or palpitations on standing?

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.text: A rising feeling in my stomach and a strange smell. No palpitations.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: Any head injury, fever, drugs or alcohol, and how did you sleep?

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.text: Three hours of sleep, and I drank a lot last night.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: Any earlier episodes, jerks or blank spells? Medical conditions, medicines, allergies, or family history of epilepsy?

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.text: None of those.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: Do you drive? What worries you most?

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.text: I drive to work. Do I have epilepsy? Will it happen again?

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: Those are fair questions. One seizure does not always mean epilepsy, and a specialist clinic will assess you. To summarise, you had a witnessed generalised seizure lasting two minutes, with a warning sensation, tongue biting and twenty minutes of confusion, after poor sleep and heavy drinking, and your glucose is normal. I will arrange bloods and a heart tracing, refer you urgently to the first seizure clinic, and go through safety advice, including driving. Any questions?

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.text: No. Thanks.

head: Task
Expected in this station
rows: Introduce yourself, check name and date of birth, start with an open question, listen, signpost, summarise and state a plan.

Witnessed two-minute generalised tonic-clonic seizure with aura (rising feeling, smell), lateral tongue bite, incontinence, 20 minutes of confusion, sleep deprivation and alcohol, no previous episodes, glucose normal.
Witness account, aura, duration, tongue bite, incontinence, recovery, head injury, fever, alcohol and drugs, sleep, previous episodes, family history, driving, work.
Say aloud: ABCDE, glucose, bloods, ECG, consider CT head, first seizure clinic referral, written safety and driving advice, no routine antiepileptic from the ED.
Acknowledge fear, stay calm, do not falsely reassure, say you would ask the senior when unsure.

head: Situation
Good response
rows: Protect from injury, time it, airway and oxygen, call for help, give a first-line benzodiazepine if beyond five minutes per protocol.
Acknowledge the loss of independence, give clear written advice, explain the specialist will review.
Thank her, reassure that she acted correctly, give simple seizure first aid advice.

head: Medical term
Say instead
rows: A sudden burst of abnormal electrical activity in the brain
A warning feeling before it starts
The confused, tired phase after a fit
A tendency to have repeated seizures
A painless test that records electrical activity of the brain

head: Question
Model reply
rows: "One seizure does not always mean epilepsy. The specialist clinic will assess you and decide."
"Not for now. You must not drive and need to tell the DVLA. The clinic will advise when it is safe."
"It might. Avoiding sleep loss and heavy alcohol helps, and the clinic will talk about your risk."
"Not usually after a first seizure. The specialist will decide after assessment."

patientQuestions.text: Tips: acknowledge the feeling first, short sentences, check understanding, no false reassurance.

examinerQuestions.question: What are your immediate actions and investigations?

items: ABCDE and glucose (done).
Bloods including electrolytes, calcium and magnesium, and ECG to exclude cardiac syncope.
Pregnancy test where relevant.
CT head if head injury, persistent deficit or other red flags.

examinerQuestions.question: How do you tell seizure from syncope?

items: Seizure: aura, longer tonic-clonic movements, lateral tongue bite, incontinence, prolonged confusion, slow recovery.
Syncope: prodrome (sweating, tunnel vision), triggers such as standing, brief jerks, rapid recovery, pallor.

examinerQuestions.question: What advice do you give at discharge?

items: Do not drive and tell the DVLA.
Avoid heights, swimming alone and baths; shower instead.
Avoid heavy alcohol and sleep loss.
Urgent first seizure clinic referral. Antiepileptic drugs are not routinely started from the ED after a first unprovoked seizure.
Give written advice and seizure first aid guidance to those at home.
Hypoglycaemia, alcohol intoxication or withdrawal, drugs.
Electrolyte disturbance, infection (meningitis, encephalitis), head injury, stroke, eclampsia.

examinerQuestionPrompts.text: Model answers are in Learning mode.

items: Missing the witness account or not separating seizure from syncope.
Not checking glucose.
No driving or safety advice, or no follow-up referral.
No summary or plan, or jargon without explanation.
A witness account is the most useful part of a first seizure history.
Check glucose and look for provoked causes.
Always give driving and safety advice.
Do not routinely start antiepileptic drugs from the ED after a first unprovoked seizure.
